ahmadiyya.1: Converts are embraced by a global family, with an instant role and hospitality.
ahmadiyya.2: Community help arrives through the same structure that records your contributions.
ahmadiyya.3: Members are promised nearness to God and burial in the Wasiyyat cemetery.
ahmadiyya.4: Drifting members are visited by office-bearers and relatives; Jalsa is the annual pull back.
ahmadiyya.5: Weak sacrifice, missed duties and an unrenewed pledge are named as spiritual failure.
ahmadiyya.6: Doubts about the system are reframed as weak faith or as the influence of enemies.
ahmadiyya.7: "No compulsion in religion" is taught, yet former members report an expected boycott.
ahmadiyya.8: Sacrifice is praised in public, and the lapsed meet silence.
ahmadiyya.9: Aam leads to Wasiyyat, which leads to new schemes, and each sacrifice exposes the next.
ahmadiyya.10: Chanda Aam is called "compulsory", yet voluntary chandas are refused from non-payers.
ahmadiyya.11: Critics are cast as disloyal and self-seeking while the system escapes audit.
ahmadiyya.12: A member complaining about an office-bearer becomes the problem for "creating disorder".
ahmadiyya.13: Duty rotas, dues and reporting become the texture of ordinary life from age seven.
ahmadiyya.14: Marriage, friendship and leisure are centered on the jamaat.
ahmadiyya.15: Family, office-bearers and the Khalifa's sermons align against a doubter.
ahmadiyya.16: Relatives and auxiliary officers carry the pressure to return or conform.
ahmadiyya.17: Organized critics are framed as conspiracies against the Jamaat.
ahmadiyya.18: Complaints about office-bearers are routed back into the same hierarchy.
ahmadiyya.19: Waqf-e-Nau children reaffirm at fifteen a pledge made for them before birth.
ahmadiyya.20: Shared persecution grief binds members to the institution itself.
ahmadiyya.21: Every route of complaint ends at an appointee of the Khalifa.
ahmadiyya.22: Marriage rules and purdah are framed as protection.
ahmadiyya.23: Adults' marriage, dress and reading are supervised by office-bearers.
ahmadiyya.24: Selfhood is defined by membership, rank of sacrifice and obedience.
ahmadiyya.25: Grievances are answered with calls for more prayer and sacrifice.
ahmadiyya.26: Contributions are fixed percentages of income, estates are pledged, and arrears are recorded.
ahmadiyya.27: Persecution news is framed as a reason to close ranks against internal critics.
ahmadiyya.28: Expulsion is published; former members report that a boycott is expected.
ahmadiyya.29: The system continues untouched; a new volunteer fills the post.
ahmadiyya.30: The institution publishes expulsion; former members report that members carry out the boycott.

anglicanism.1: It appears in some evangelical outreach, such as Alpha courses, but not in most parishes.
anglicanism.2: Published school admissions criteria can favor worshipping families.
anglicanism.3: Eternal life is promised, and for clergy, a future of ministry.
anglicanism.4: Weak here: families who come for the occasional offices are invited back.
anglicanism.5: Some traditions use the language of sin, and decline is blamed on parishes.
anglicanism.6: Survivors being told processes were followed when they were not is not recorded.
anglicanism.7: Women may be bishops; parishes may reject their oversight.
anglicanism.8: Preferment (promotion to senior posts) and patronage shape clerical careers.
anglicanism.9: Independent safeguarding was promised, redesigned and phased.
anglicanism.10: Doctrinal breadth lets any position be "one tradition".
anglicanism.11: Critics of process are cast as hostile to the church.
anglicanism.12: Complainants were treated as reputational threats (per IICSA and Makin).
anglicanism.13: Deference to senior clergy was normalized (IICSA; Gibb).
anglicanism.14: Historically, isolation happened in closed camps and choir environments.
anglicanism.15: Complaints are routed between parish, diocese and national bodies.
anglicanism.16: Weak here: congregations show loyalty to accused clergy.
anglicanism.17: IICSA found survivors' accounts were disbelieved in documented cases.
anglicanism.18: The church was slow to respond to survivors (IICSA).
anglicanism.19: Clergy must make the Declaration of Assent to doctrine and discipline, with the house attached.
anglicanism.20: No example is recorded yet; research is needed.
anglicanism.21: Survivors' repeated complaints failed (IICSA), but helplessness is not an inquiry finding.
anglicanism.22: Oversight of clergy lives runs through the bishop's licence and the tied house.
anglicanism.23: Weak here: a culture of deference prevails.
anglicanism.24: Clergy identity is fused with the post.
anglicanism.25: IICSA recorded evidence that some victims may have been pressured to forgive their abuser.
anglicanism.26: For clergy it is codified, working through the parish share and the tied house.
anglicanism.27: The decline narrative is used to justify closures.
anglicanism.28: Licence withdrawal ends ministry and home.
anglicanism.29: The benefice is merged and the post re-advertised.
anglicanism.30: Responsibility is deflected as "a matter for the diocese".

bahai.1: Seekers are welcomed with unity language, interfaith warmth, firesides and consultation.
bahai.2: Baháʼí communities may offer warmth through firesides, study circles and classes.
bahai.3: The Baháʼí Faith offers a sweeping future of world unity, peace and racial harmony.
bahai.4: Someone distancing may be gently contacted with invitations to firesides.
bahai.5: The Baháʼí Faith can devalue dissent by framing criticism as disunity, ego or impatience.
bahai.6: A person criticizes administration and is told they are harming unity.
bahai.7: Investigation must arrive at the Covenant; dissent risks shunning as a covenant-breaker.
bahai.8: Service is rewarded irregularly with appointment or mention, so believers serve more.
bahai.9: A seeker is welcomed through unity, but the standard shifts to obeying administration.
bahai.10: "Independent investigation" is stressed to seekers, then covenant loyalty becomes central.
bahai.11: Baháʼí institutions may accuse critics of disunity while avoiding accountability.
bahai.12: A person questions administration, and the first response may deny coercion.
bahai.13: Service expectations become normal through study circles, teaching plans and unity.
bahai.14: Baháʼí isolation is often soft: community activities gradually become the social world.
bahai.15: Baháʼí triangulation can run through Spiritual Assemblies and the House of Justice.
bahai.16: A Baháʼí who questions administration may be approached by assembly members and friends.
bahai.17: Critics of administration may be described as disunified, ego-driven or impatient.
bahai.18: A member raises concerns and is redirected to consultation, patience and unity.
bahai.19: Seekers consent to a faith of unity, then meet administrative obedience.
bahai.20: A member feels distress when dissent threatens unity, then relief on returning to harmony.
bahai.21: A member raises concerns but is repeatedly redirected into consultation and patience.
bahai.22: Administrative obedience is framed as unity.
bahai.23: Members who dissent may be treated as impatient or not understanding the Covenant.
bahai.24: The person's identity may be absorbed into unity, service, administration and the future.
bahai.26: Baháʼí financial control may appear as moral pressure to support the Faith's growth.
bahai.27: Baháʼí communities may manufacture crisis around disunity, dissent and failure to serve.
bahai.28: A member who publicly criticizes administration may be treated as disunified or immature.
bahai.29: A member who stops serving is replaced by someone eager for study circles.
bahai.30: Seekers hear of independent investigation; after enrollment dissent may meet obedience.

buddhism.1: Newcomers are met with calm voices, meditation cushions, tea and the promise of peace.
buddhism.2: Buddhist centers may offer meditation, retreats, tea and a peaceful refuge.
buddhism.3: Buddhism can future-fake through enlightenment, nirvana, better rebirth and merit.
buddhism.4: A student leaving may be told they are running from suffering or clinging to ego.
buddhism.5: Institutional Buddhism can devalue by defining ordinary desire as the root of suffering.
buddhism.6: A student says a teacher was abusive and hears, "Notice your aversion."
buddhism.7: Students are told to test the teachings, but negative findings are diagnosed as ego.
buddhism.8: Breakthroughs credit the method and teacher; dry months indicate your hindrances.
buddhism.9: A seeker begins meditation, then must attend retreats and stop trusting anger.
buddhism.10: "Nonattachment" can mean freedom from craving, but also suppression or tolerance of abuse.
buddhism.11: A teacher may accuse a questioning student of ego, shielded by robes and titles.
buddhism.12: A student reports teacher abuse, and the sangha may deny it or cite skillful means.
buddhism.13: Practitioners can become desensitized to reading pain as attachment and anger as ego.
buddhism.14: Buddhism can isolate through sangha dependence, retreat culture and teacher authority.
buddhism.15: Buddhism can triangulate through teacher, sangha, lineage and senior students.
buddhism.16: A harmed student may hear from senior students: "You are attached to anger."
buddhism.17: A student reporting teacher abuse may be labeled angry, attached, egoic or unstable.
buddhism.18: A student reports teacher abuse and is told to sit with anger and examine projection.
buddhism.19: A student "chooses" teacher authority after being taught that resistance is ego.
buddhism.20: The teacher names craving and ego as the cause, then offers meditation as relief.
buddhism.21: A student repeatedly names harm and is told to examine attachment, anger, projection, and ego.
buddhism.22: Teachers may control through compassion language: "This is practice."
buddhism.23: Students may be treated as spiritually immature if they trust anger, grief or moral alarm.
buddhism.24: Buddhist practice can erode identity by turning desire, anger and selfhood into problems.
buddhism.26: Buddhist centers may rely on dana, retreat fees, book sales and unpaid service.
buddhism.27: Communities may manufacture crisis by framing departure as running from suffering.
buddhism.28: A student who reports teacher abuse may be quietly excluded from sangha spaces.
buddhism.29: A student who reports abuse leaves; new retreatants arrive and are told nothing.
buddhism.30: Anger is welcome as something to observe, but anger at the teacher becomes ego.

catholicism.1: A wounded person is folded into parish life with the promise of finally belonging.
catholicism.2: Catholic parishes, schools and charities often provide real material help.
catholicism.3: Catholicism offers a massive future economy: heaven, purgatory, indulgences and sainthood.
catholicism.4: A lapsed Catholic may be approached with guilt-heavy language like "Come home".
catholicism.5: Catholicism can devalue through inherited guilt, original sin, mortal sin and shame.
catholicism.6: Questioning clerical authority gets "You are rejecting the Church Christ founded".
catholicism.7: A conscience contradicting the Magisterium is taught to be malformed.
catholicism.8: Grace arrives through sacraments the institution meters, and the peace wears off.
catholicism.9: A Catholic receives absolution, but the shame remains and deeper repentance is needed.
catholicism.10: Catholic teaching can sound absolute in doctrine but flexible in pastoral application.
catholicism.11: Catholic hierarchy may accuse critics of attacking the Church.
catholicism.12: Clerical abuse is denied, minimized, transferred, buried in process or reframed.
catholicism.13: Children may be normalized early into confession, mortal sin, guilt and penance.
catholicism.14: Catholic isolation often works through institutional authority and warnings against error.
catholicism.15: You are rarely just disagreeing with a local priest, but with the Church across centuries.
catholicism.16: A lapsed Catholic is pressured by parents, priests and relatives: "Go to confession".
catholicism.17: Critics of clerical abuse may be framed as anti-Catholic, rebellious or secularized.
catholicism.18: Abuse survivors may face diocesan bureaucracy, canonical process and institutional delay.
catholicism.19: Children receive sacraments before they can understand what Catholic identity implies.
catholicism.20: Catholicism can bind people through guilt and relief, from mortal sin to absolution.
catholicism.21: A Catholic tries confession, penance and obedience but still feels unworthy.
catholicism.22: Catholic authority presents restrictions on sexuality and marriage as loving guidance.
catholicism.23: Priests are called Father and the Church Mother, so laypeople remain spiritual children.
catholicism.24: Catholic identity can absorb the person through sacrament, family, school and parish.
catholicism.25: Suffering is bypassed through "offer it up", penance and obedience.
catholicism.26: Catholic financial control can appear through parish giving, tuition and diocesan appeals.
catholicism.27: Catholic crisis language may center secularism, moral collapse and attacks on the family.
catholicism.28: A Catholic who challenges clerical abuse may be treated as lapsed or rebellious.
catholicism.29: A questioning layperson leaves, and parish life continues with another volunteer.
catholicism.30: If conscience agrees with Church authority it is conscience, and if not, malformed.

christianity.1: A grieving visitor is told, "God brought you here" and "You're home now."
christianity.2: After a church helps, a questioner hears, "After everything this church has done for you."
christianity.3: Heaven is presented as the ultimate deferred reward: no more tears, reunion, eternal joy.
christianity.4: After you stop attending, texts ask, "We miss you" and "Is everything okay spiritually?"
christianity.5: Christianity often begins by telling the person they are a sinner before God.
christianity.6: A person says, "This church hurt me," and is told, "Don't let bitterness take root."
christianity.7: Members must test everything against Scripture, but a different conclusion is wrong.
christianity.8: Worship is engineered for peaks, and dry Sundays are framed as your hidden sin.
christianity.9: "Just accept Jesus" becomes baptism, membership, tithing, serving and submission.
christianity.10: "God's will" is kept vague enough to justify almost anything, even forgiving abuse.
christianity.11: Churches accuse wounded members of being "divisive" after leadership created the division.
christianity.12: A survivor reports abuse, and the church says it did not happen, then calls them bitter.
christianity.13: A believer is trained to accept weekly self-denigration until it sounds like worship.
christianity.14: Christianity can isolate through warnings against "the world" and "bad company".
christianity.15: Questioners are sent to elders and mentors who all say: submit, forgive, stay.
christianity.16: The pastor does not confront; small-group leaders and "concerned friends" text instead.
christianity.17: A church labels a critic bitter, divisive, rebellious, or under demonic attack.
christianity.18: Leaders say they are "looking into it," then weeks or months pass with no update.
christianity.19: A teenager "chooses" baptism after years of hell teaching and fear of being unsaved.
christianity.20: The church teaches you are sinful, then offers forgiveness and "the peace of God."
christianity.21: A member with hard questions is told to pray, submit, wait and stop doubting.
christianity.22: Leaders tell members not to date unbelievers or hear critics, to "guard their hearts."
christianity.23: Adult believers are called sheep needing shepherds, or children needing spiritual fathers.
christianity.24: The believer's identity is replaced with categories: sinner, saved, servant, sheep.
christianity.25: Abuse is bypassed with "forgive seventy times seven" or "vengeance is the Lord's."
christianity.26: Churches may pressure members to tithe, give offerings and volunteer unpaid labor.
christianity.27: Churches may manufacture crisis through hell, demons, spiritual warfare and end-times.
christianity.28: A church that called someone "family" quietly stops inviting them after they question it.
christianity.29: A volunteer leaves after burnout; the church recruits another: "God providing."
christianity.30: A pastor never says "Shun her," but preaches about wolves and divisive people.

confucianism.1: A person is welcomed into a moral universe of order, family, respect and social harmony.
confucianism.2: Confucian systems offer social stability: family duty, elder care, education, hierarchy.
confucianism.3: Obey roles and sacrifice desire now, and the family or society will flourish later.
confucianism.4: Resisting expectations may be met with filial guilt: "After all your parents sacrificed."
confucianism.5: Confucian systems can devalue the individual beneath role: child, parent, elder, subject.
confucianism.6: A child says parental control is oppressive, and the response is, “You are ungrateful.”
confucianism.7: The child of a harmful parent must choose between the lie that honors and the truth.
confucianism.8: Elder approval is dispensed sparingly; a lifetime of duty may earn one deathbed sentence.
confucianism.9: A child obeys parents, then obedience becomes career choice, marriage choice, elder care.
confucianism.10: "Respect" can mean courtesy, obedience, silence, or family reputation.
confucianism.11: Elders may accuse younger people of selfishness for choosing their own marriage or career.
confucianism.12: An adult child names parental control, and the family calls it love, sacrifice or duty.
confucianism.13: Children are normalized into hierarchy early: elders speak, children obey.
confucianism.14: Confucian isolation works through family hierarchy, filial piety and demands for harmony.
confucianism.15: Confucian triangulation is often family-based: parents, elders, ancestors and family name.
confucianism.16: An adult child resisting family control may be pressured by parents, elders and relatives.
confucianism.17: Adult children setting boundaries may be smeared as ungrateful, selfish or disrespectful.
confucianism.18: Adult children ask for boundaries and hear silence, shame or "after all we did for you."
confucianism.19: Adult children "choose" careers and roles after years of filial debt and guilt.
confucianism.20: Family systems can bond through guilt and relief: "After all we did for you."
confucianism.21: Adult children setting boundaries meet tears, silence, shame and charges of ingratitude.
confucianism.22: Parents control career, marriage and religion under the language of love and harmony.
confucianism.23: Adult children remain “children” in the family hierarchy no matter their age.
confucianism.24: The person is defined by role: child, parent, spouse, elder, student, ancestor.
confucianism.25: Abuse or control is bypassed as filial piety.
confucianism.26: Family financial control may appear through tuition, housing, inheritance and elder care.
confucianism.27: Families may manufacture crisis around marriage, career, elder respect and reputation.
confucianism.28: Adult children who reject expectations may meet silence, shame or inheritance threats.
confucianism.29: A noncompliant adult child is emotionally replaced by a more obedient sibling or cousin.
confucianism.30: Parents say they only advise, while money, guilt and inheritance enforce compliance.

dawoodi-bohra.1: The community offers a warm, total embrace.
dawoodi-bohra.2: Loans and housing come from the office that disciplines.
dawoodi-bohra.3: Salvation is taught as coming through allegiance to the Daʿi.
dawoodi-bohra.4: Families pull back those who drift.
dawoodi-bohra.5: Breaches of the misaq are framed as spiritual failure.
dawoodi-bohra.6: Khatna is minimized as harmless against survivors' testimony.
dawoodi-bohra.7: An oath is sworn before adulthood and binds for life.
dawoodi-bohra.8: Favor and permissions go to loyal families.
dawoodi-bohra.9: Khatna is a "religious rite" at home and "follow the law" abroad.
dawoodi-bohra.10: No written renunciation of khatna covering every country is recorded on this page.
dawoodi-bohra.12: Survivors who speak out are accused of defaming the community.
dawoodi-bohra.13: Khatna, most often at six or seven, is treated as a family rite.
dawoodi-bohra.14: Business, marriage and burial take place inside the community.
dawoodi-bohra.15: The mother-in-law, the ʿamil and the community align.
dawoodi-bohra.17: Reformers are vilified and assaulted, per the 1979 testimony.
dawoodi-bohra.18: Litigation ran for decades before any reconsideration.
dawoodi-bohra.19: The misaq is taken before adulthood.
dawoodi-bohra.20: Shared grief (Muharram) and belonging bind members to the office.
dawoodi-bohra.21: Reformist accounts say every life event needs permission.
dawoodi-bohra.22: Permissions are framed as spiritual care.
dawoodi-bohra.23: Adults seek permission for life events.
dawoodi-bohra.25: Harm is answered with calls for loyalty.
dawoodi-bohra.26: Reformist accounts tie dues to permissions.
dawoodi-bohra.27: Outside threats are cited against reformers.
dawoodi-bohra.29: The office and the community continue unchanged.
dawoodi-bohra.30: No source records responsibility placed on families rather than the institution.

eastern-orthodoxy.1: The convert is enchanted by incense, icons, chanting, liturgy and ancientness.
eastern-orthodoxy.2: Converts may receive intense hospitality, from meals after liturgy to spiritual direction.
eastern-orthodoxy.3: Orthodoxy offers theosis, becoming united with God, and so a powerful hook.
eastern-orthodoxy.4: Those who leave Orthodoxy may be told they are abandoning the fullness of the faith.
eastern-orthodoxy.5: Eastern Orthodoxy can devalue through relentless emphasis on the passions and pride.
eastern-orthodoxy.6: A convert senses authoritarian control, and the response is "That is your pride".
eastern-orthodoxy.7: Converts are told Orthodoxy is freedom from legalism, then handed fasting rules.
eastern-orthodoxy.8: The fading glow is diagnosed as a slackening prayer rule, so the rule thickens.
eastern-orthodoxy.9: Converts are first told "Come and see", then they must fast, confess and obey a priest.
eastern-orthodoxy.10: Orthodoxy often says it is not legalistic, yet believers may face strict expectations.
eastern-orthodoxy.11: Orthodoxy may accuse converts who leave of pride, while demanding deep submission.
eastern-orthodoxy.12: A parishioner reports clerical control and is told "You are prideful".
eastern-orthodoxy.13: Converts are slowly accustomed to fasting cycles, confession and long liturgies.
eastern-orthodoxy.14: Eastern Orthodoxy can isolate converts by teaching them to distrust Western Christianity.
eastern-orthodoxy.15: Orthodoxy triangulates through spiritual fathers, saints and "the mind of the Church".
eastern-orthodoxy.16: A questioning convert hears concern about pride from priest, godparent and elders.
eastern-orthodoxy.17: A person leaving Orthodoxy may be labeled proud, spiritually deluded or unstable.
eastern-orthodoxy.18: Concerns about priestly control are met with a private talk with the priest.
eastern-orthodoxy.19: Converts "freely" enter Orthodoxy after being told it is the fullness of the faith.
eastern-orthodoxy.20: Orthodoxy calls itself a hospital for the soul while stressing sickness and unworthiness.
eastern-orthodoxy.21: A believer tries questioning and is told that questioning proves delusion.
eastern-orthodoxy.22: The Church is framed as a hospital for the soul, and priests as physicians.
eastern-orthodoxy.23: The spiritual father model can position adult believers as patients or children.
eastern-orthodoxy.24: Converts may gradually replace their previous identity with an Orthodox convert identity.
eastern-orthodoxy.25: Pain is bypassed through humility, repentance, obedience and fasting.
eastern-orthodoxy.26: Orthodox parishes may rely on donations, stewardship pledges and building funds.
eastern-orthodoxy.27: Orthodoxy may frame the modern West as spiritually diseased.
eastern-orthodoxy.28: A convert celebrated as having "come home" may be dismissed as prideful after leaving.
eastern-orthodoxy.29: A convert leaves; another convert arrives, enchanted by icons, incense, chant, and ancientness.
eastern-orthodoxy.30: Orthodoxy can say "We do not have a legalistic rule system" while pressuring fasting.

hare-krishna.1: Newcomers are drawn in by chanting, prasadam, music and the promise of joyful devotion.
hare-krishna.2: ISKCON often offers prasadam, chanting, festivals, music and joyful devotional atmosphere.
hare-krishna.3: ISKCON future-fakes through return to Godhead, liberation, and eternal service to Krishna.
hare-krishna.4: Someone leaving ISKCON may be pulled back through prasadam, kirtan and devotee friends.
hare-krishna.5: ISKCON can devalue ordinary identity by calling material life illusion, or maya.
hare-krishna.6: A devotee says temple life is exploitative, and the response is, “That is maya testing you.”
hare-krishna.7: Reluctance to serve Krishna is called maya, so its absence is diagnosed and corrected.
hare-krishna.8: Some nights kirtan lifts the room, some it doesn't; Krishna's choosing explains both.
hare-krishna.9: A newcomer who enjoys prasadam must then chant rounds, serve, donate and surrender.
hare-krishna.10: Guru authority is devotion when attractive, individual imperfection when abuse is exposed.
hare-krishna.11: ISKCON communities may accuse leavers of being captured by maya.
hare-krishna.12: A devotee reports abuse, and the response may deny it or call it isolated imperfection.
hare-krishna.13: Newcomers are slowly normalized into the temple schedule, diet and guru devotion.
hare-krishna.14: ISKCON can isolate through temple life and warnings against materialistic association.
hare-krishna.15: ISKCON triangulates through guru, temple president, senior devotees and fear of maya.
hare-krishna.16: A questioning devotee may be approached by senior devotees, temple leaders and friends.
hare-krishna.17: Former devotees may be labeled fallen, offensive, in maya, or lacking surrender.
hare-krishna.18: A devotee who questions guru authority is told to chant more and avoid offenses.
hare-krishna.19: Newcomers "choose" devotional life after immersion in chanting, prasadam and warmth.
hare-krishna.20: ISKCON can bond through sweetness and shame, paired with devaluation of material life.
hare-krishna.21: A burned-out devotee is told to chant more, serve more purely, and surrender.
hare-krishna.22: Guru obedience, temple service and diet are framed as loving purification.
hare-krishna.23: Devotees may be treated as fallen if they desire ordinary family, romance or autonomy.
hare-krishna.24: Devotee identity replaces ordinary identity: servant of Krishna, follower of guru.
hare-krishna.26: ISKCON financial control may appear through donations, book distribution and temple labor.
hare-krishna.27: ISKCON may manufacture crisis around maya, bad association and leaving devotional service.
hare-krishna.28: A devotee who leaves may be described as fallen, in maya, or lacking surrender.
hare-krishna.29: A devotee who leaves is replaced by a newcomer drawn by kirtan and prasadam.
hare-krishna.30: ISKCON can say temple life is voluntary while outside life is called maya.

hinduism.1: Seekers are drawn by yoga, temples, gurus, festivals and the promise all paths are valid.
hinduism.2: Temples and ashrams may provide food, festivals, community support and guru guidance.
hinduism.3: Hindu traditions can future-fake through moksha, better rebirth and guru blessing.
hinduism.4: A person leaving may be told they are abandoning dharma or creating bad karma.
hinduism.5: Hindu institutional systems can devalue through karma, caste, purity and guru hierarchy.
hinduism.6: A person questions caste or guru authority and is told they do not understand dharma.
hinduism.7: All paths are valid, but leaving this guru's path shows their karma is not ripe.
hinduism.8: Darshan is structured scarcity: long queues, brief contact, rarity as proof of potency.
hinduism.9: A person fulfills family rituals, then must also obey caste, marriage and purity rules.
hinduism.10: Caste may be called spiritual order, social custom or irrelevant ideal, depending on criticism.
hinduism.11: Caste-based systems may accuse lower-status people of impurity while protecting hierarchy.
hinduism.12: A person challenges caste discrimination; the response may call it culture.
hinduism.13: Ritual, caste expectations and purity rules feel normal because family life embeds them.
hinduism.14: Hindu isolation may operate through family, caste, marriage rules and temple networks.
hinduism.15: Hindu triangulation can run through parents, caste networks, gurus, astrologers, priests.
hinduism.16: A person resisting caste expectations may be pressured by parents, relatives and priests.
hinduism.17: Critics of caste may be labeled anti-Hindu, Westernized, colonized, or ignorant of dharma.
hinduism.18: A person challenges caste and is told, "This is tradition" or "do not disrespect elders."
hinduism.19: A young adult "chooses" arranged marriage after family honor and caste narrow the field.
hinduism.20: Family, caste, karma and guru authority can create cycles of shame and relief.
hinduism.21: A person challenges caste or guru authority and is told it is karma, dharma or tradition.

mirror.1: After the failure, you flood yourself with promises that everything changes now.
mirror.2: You give until you are empty, then keep score against yourself for not being further along.
mirror.3: You promise yourself that life starts when you lose the weight or get the promotion.
mirror.4: You leave the habit, then pull yourself back with "maybe it wasn't that bad."
mirror.5: The voice inside says you are not enough, and it was installed by the systems you lived in.
mirror.6: You tell yourself "it wasn't that bad" while your body still remembers that it was.
mirror.7: You rest and feel guilty, then work and feel resentful, so both choices punish you.
mirror.8: You feel good about yourself one day and worthless the next, with nothing in between changed.
mirror.9: You achieve the thing, and the next goal appears before you can feel it was enough.
mirror.10: You tell yourself "I'm fine" and "it is what it is," so nothing ever has to change.
mirror.11: You call the coworker "lazy" because you are terrified of your own need for rest.
mirror.12: You name the harm, then attack yourself for being dramatic and playing the victim.
mirror.13: The exhaustion and the loneliness are no longer alarming, because you normalized them.
mirror.14: You cancel the plan and let the friendship go quiet so no one gets close enough to leave.
mirror.15: You compare yourself to a stranger on the feed whose life looks like the one you should have.
mirror.16: When you are about to set a boundary, your mother's voice in your head says "that's selfish."
mirror.17: You tell the story of your own life with the system's edits, and you are always the problem.
mirror.18: The grief arrives and you scroll, ignoring your own body's signals.
mirror.19: You point to "I chose this" as proof that everything that followed was wanted.
mirror.20: You return to your own suffering because it is the most familiar thing in your life.
mirror.21: You tell yourself "I can't change" because every system punished your attempts to try.
mirror.22: You restrict the food and override the exhaustion, then call the control discipline.
mirror.23: You Google the answer before you check what your own body already knows.

mirror.26: You tell yourself "I can't afford to rest" and deny yourself even the small things.

mirror.28: You stop mentioning the book you were going to write, and no one mourns the dream.
mirror.29: You replace yourself with another diet and another plan instead of becoming whole.
mirror.30: You tell yourself "I'm just tired" so you never have to see the pattern you are in.
